specPoints.text: understand how to classify reactions of organic compounds as substitution, addition and combustion knowledge of reaction mechanisms is not required

primer.text: From Naming Organic Compounds you already know how stems and suffixes label every molecule in this topic. This note sorts the reactions those molecules undergo into three named types, each with an equation you can already balance, and sets the sorting habit the rest of the topic uses.

lessons.title: Substitution and addition
lessons.opening: Organic reactions fall into three named types, and the first two differ by what joins and what leaves. This lesson contrasts a swap of one group for another with molecules combining into a single larger product.
keyPoints: Substitution happens when one functional group or atom in a molecule is replaced by another.
Methane reacting with bromine in ultraviolet light substitutes one hydrogen for bromine, giving bromomethane and HBr.
Addition happens when two or more molecules combine into one larger molecule with no other products.
Bromine adds across the C=C double bond of ethene to give dibromoethane, C2H4Br2.
No mechanisms are needed at this level, only the classification of each reaction by type.

low.restatement: Substitution swaps something out: one atom or group leaves and another takes its place. Addition combines: two molecules become one bigger molecule and nothing else is made. Count the products after the change: one merged product means addition, two products mean a swap has happened.
low.analogy: Substitution is swapping a seat on a bus; addition is two puzzle pieces clicking into one picture with no leftover pieces anywhere.
low.examPointer: Look for the giveaway signs: two products beside an arrow suggests substitution, one product only suggests addition.

medium.restatement: A substitution reaction replaces one functional group or atom with another, as when methane and bromine form bromomethane and hydrogen bromide under ultraviolet light. An addition reaction merges two or more molecules into a single larger molecule with no other products, as when bromine adds across the double bond of ethene to form dibromoethane.
medium.analogy: Substitution is a like-for-like player swap mid-match, while addition is two teams merging into one squad roster with nobody released: count the players after the change and the difference is obvious.
medium.examPointer: Name the type, then justify it from the equation: replacement with two products is substitution, one merged product is addition.

check.stem: Methane reacts with bromine under ultraviolet light to give bromomethane and hydrogen bromide. Which type of reaction is this?

options.text: Substitution, because a hydrogen atom is replaced by bromine
options.explanation: One atom in the methane is swapped for another, which is the defining move of a substitution reaction.

options.text: Addition, because the molecules combine
options.explanation: Two products form here; addition would leave one merged product and nothing else.

options.text: Combustion, because bromine is reactive
options.explanation: Combustion means burning in oxygen; no oxygen takes part in this reaction.

options.text: No classification applies without a mechanism
options.explanation: Mechanisms are not required; the type follows from what the equation shows.

check.stem: What is the defining feature of an addition reaction?

options.text: Two or more molecules form one larger molecule with no other products
options.explanation: Everything that enters the reaction leaves inside the single merged product.

options.text: One atom swaps places with another inside the molecule
options.explanation: That describes substitution, which produces two products rather than one.

options.text: The molecule burns in a plentiful oxygen supply
options.explanation: Burning in oxygen is combustion, the third type, not addition.

options.text: A catalyst is always required for the reaction to proceed
options.explanation: Addition needs no catalyst in general; the definition is about merging molecules.

check.stem: Ethene reacts with bromine to give C2H4Br2. Why is this an addition reaction?

options.text: Both bromine atoms add across the double bond, leaving one product
options.explanation: The two reactant molecules merge into dibromoethane alone, which is the addition signature.

options.text: Because ethene is an alkane with strong bonds
options.explanation: Ethene is an alkene, and the classification rests on the single merged product.

options.text: Because a hydrogen atom was replaced by bromine
options.explanation: No hydrogen leaves the molecule here; the bromine joins on across the double bond.

options.text: Because the reaction needs ultraviolet light to start
options.explanation: Ultraviolet light belongs to the alkane-halogen substitution story, not this addition.

check.stem: How many products does a substitution reaction produce from one organic molecule and one attacking molecule?

options.text: Two products: the substituted molecule and the displaced fragment
options.explanation: What leaves the organic molecule pairs with the incoming atom to form the second product, as in HBr.

options.text: One product only, because everything merges
options.explanation: One merged product describes addition; substitution always has something displaced.

options.text: Three products in every case
options.explanation: The standard substitution makes exactly two products at this level.

options.text: It depends on the temperature used
options.explanation: The product count follows from the reaction type, not the temperature.

check.stem: Do you need to know reaction mechanisms for this classification work?

options.text: No, classifying as substitution, addition or combustion is enough
options.explanation: The specification explicitly excludes mechanisms; naming the type is the required skill.

options.text: Yes, every classification needs the full mechanism quoted
options.explanation: Mechanisms are beyond the requirement; the type label alone is the marking point.

options.text: Only for addition reactions
options.explanation: No reaction type at this level demands a mechanism for classification.

options.text: Only when the reaction happens in sunlight
options.explanation: Light conditions help identify substitution, but mechanisms stay excluded everywhere.

lessons.title: Combustion: complete and incomplete
lessons.opening: The third reaction type is burning, and its products depend entirely on how much oxygen is available. This lesson separates the complete and incomplete versions and shows the balancing on methane and propane.
keyPoints: Combustion is the scientific term for burning an organic substance in oxygen.
Complete combustion happens with an unlimited supply of air or oxygen, giving carbon dioxide and water.
Methane burns completely as CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O, and propane as C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O.
Incomplete combustion happens in a limited oxygen supply, giving carbon monoxide or carbon plus water.
Methane in short oxygen supply gives CO + H2O, or even carbon soot, instead of carbon dioxide.

low.restatement: Burning with plenty of oxygen gives carbon dioxide and water. Burning with little oxygen gives carbon monoxide or carbon soot as well as water. The oxygen supply in the appliance decides which of the two outcomes you get.
low.analogy: A well-ventilated campfire leaves white ash, while a smothered one leaves black soot; oxygen supply decides what the fuel turns into.
low.examPointer: State the oxygen supply and the products together; naming one without the other loses the marking point.

medium.restatement: In unlimited air or oxygen an organic substance burns completely, forming carbon dioxide and water, as the methane and propane equations show. When oxygen is limited the same fuels burn incompletely, producing carbon monoxide or carbon alongside water, which is why the methane equation can yield CO instead of CO2.
medium.analogy: Oxygen is the currency that pays for full oxidation: with a rich wallet every carbon buys a full dioxide, but a poor wallet forces carbon to settle for monoxide or plain soot.
medium.examPointer: Balance the combustion equation from the fuel formula, then check the oxygen supply described before choosing CO2 or CO as the carbon product.

check.stem: What are the products when methane burns completely in air?

options.text: Carbon dioxide and water
options.explanation: Unlimited oxygen oxidises every carbon fully to CO2, with hydrogen ending as water.

options.text: Carbon monoxide and water
options.explanation: Carbon monoxide belongs to incomplete burning in a limited oxygen supply.

options.text: Carbon and hydrogen only
options.explanation: With oxygen present the products are oxides, not the bare elements.

options.text: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen gas
options.explanation: Hydrogen from the fuel joins oxygen to make water, not hydrogen gas.

check.stem: Which condition produces carbon monoxide during the burning of a hydrocarbon?

options.text: A limited supply of air or oxygen
options.explanation: Starved of oxygen, the carbon cannot fully oxidise and settles for monoxide.

options.text: An unlimited supply of oxygen
options.explanation: Plentiful oxygen drives complete burning to carbon dioxide instead.

options.text: The presence of nitrogen in the air
options.explanation: Nitrogen is already in air during complete burning too; only the oxygen shortage matters.

options.text: Any temperature below 100 degrees Celsius
options.explanation: Temperature alone does not decide the products; the oxygen supply does.

check.stem: Balance the complete equation: CH4 + ? O2 -> CO2 + ? H2O

options.text: 2 before O2 and 2 before H2O
options.explanation: Four hydrogens need two waters, and those two waters plus CO2 need four oxygens, so 2O2 supplies them.

options.text: 1 before O2 and 2 before H2O
options.explanation: One O2 gives only two oxygens, but CO2 and 2H2O together need four.

options.text: 2 before O2 and 1 before H2O
options.explanation: One water leaves two hydrogens stranded from the four that methane carries.

options.text: 4 before O2 and 4 before H2O
options.explanation: That over-supplies oxygen and breaks the atom balance the equation must keep.

check.stem: In an oxygen-poor appliance, what can form from methane instead of carbon dioxide?

options.text: Carbon monoxide, or carbon soot in very poor supply
options.explanation: The note shows both routes: 2CH4 + 3O2 to CO, and CH4 + O2 all the way down to carbon.

options.text: Sulfur dioxide, from the methane itself
options.explanation: Methane carries no sulfur; SO2 arises from impurities in other fuels.

options.text: Nothing, because methane cannot burn without full oxygen
options.explanation: Incomplete burning is still burning; it simply stops at CO or carbon.

options.text: Only water, with the carbon vanishing
options.explanation: Atoms are conserved; the carbon must appear as CO, soot or CO2, never vanish.

check.stem: Why is combustion classified alongside substitution and addition?

options.text: Because it is one of the three named types of organic reaction
options.explanation: The classification scheme of the topic lists exactly these three reaction families.

options.text: Because it only happens to alkanes
options.explanation: The note records alkenes burning too, so the type is not alkane-only.

options.text: Because it needs ultraviolet light like substitution
options.explanation: Combustion needs oxygen and a flame or spark, not ultraviolet radiation.

options.text: Because it produces one merged product
options.explanation: Two products, CO2 and water, form in complete burning, so it is not an addition case.

glossary.definition: A reaction in which one atom or functional group in a molecule is replaced by another.
A reaction in which two or more molecules combine into one larger molecule with no other products.
The scientific term for burning, in which a substance reacts with oxygen giving out heat.
Burning with unlimited oxygen, producing carbon dioxide and water only.
Burning with limited oxygen, producing carbon monoxide or carbon soot as well as water.

workedExample.prompt: Classify each reaction and justify your answer: a) CH4 + Br2 → CH3Br + HBr (in UV light); b) C2H4 + Br2 → C2H4Br2; c) CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O; d) CH4 + 3/2 O2 → CO + 2H2O.
steps: a) Substitution: one hydrogen atom of methane is replaced by bromine, and two products form — bromomethane and hydrogen bromide.
b) Addition: two molecules combine into one larger molecule with no other products — both bromine atoms add across ethene's C=C double bond.
c) Complete combustion: burning in an unlimited supply of oxygen, giving carbon dioxide and water only.
d) Incomplete combustion: in a limited oxygen supply, carbon monoxide forms instead of carbon dioxide (alongside water).
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Substitution (replacement; two products). b) Addition (one merged product). c) Complete combustion. d) Incomplete combustion.
